item.title: Writing Better Commit Messages
item.description:
The Cost of Bad Commit Messages

Open any long-running codebase and run git log. What do you see? “fix bug,” “wip,” “asdf,” “update,” “final,” “final2.” These messages tell you nothing about why a change was made, what problem it solved, or what context you’d need to understand it six months later.

When you’re debugging a regression at midnight, a commit message that reads “fix null pointer in user session lookup after token expiry” is worth considerably more than “bug fix.”

item.title: Exploring Patagonia
item.description:
Getting There Is Part of It

Patagonia doesn’t let you arrive easily. The nearest city with reliable international flights is Punta Arenas, a three-hour bus ride from Puerto Natales, which is itself a two-hour drive from Torres del Paine National Park. The journey is part of the experience — you arrive having already traveled through a landscape that feels progressively more remote, more windswept, more like the edge of something.

item.title: Building a Home Lab
item.description:
Why Bother?

Running your own infrastructure at home sounds like a lot of work — because it is, sometimes. But the payoff is substantial: you learn by doing things that managed services hide from you, you control your own data, and you get a sandbox that nobody will fire you for breaking.

My motivation was simple: I wanted to understand Kubernetes properly, and running it in a real (if small) cluster taught me more in two weeks than months of documentation reading.

item.title: The Science of Sleep
item.description:
Sleep Is Not Rest

The popular image of sleep as a kind of nightly reboot — brain off, body idle — is wrong. During sleep, your brain is arguably more active in certain respects than during waking hours. It’s consolidating memories, clearing metabolic waste, regulating hormones, and running maintenance on neural connections. Far from downtime, sleep is when a lot of the important work happens.

item.title: Coffee Brewing Methods Compared
item.description:
It Starts With the Bean

Every brewing method amplifies certain characteristics of the coffee you’re using. A bright, lightly roasted Ethiopian natural will taste entirely different through a Chemex than through an espresso machine — not because one is better, but because each method extracts differently. Understanding that relationship is more useful than chasing the “best” method.

The Main Contenders

French Press

Profile: Full-bodied, rich, slightly silty.

The metal filter lets oils and fine particles through, producing a heavier cup than paper-filtered methods. Forgiving with grind size and timing. Best with medium-to-dark roasts where you want texture and weight.

item.title: Fermentation and Gut Health
item.description:
The Gut Microbiome, Briefly

Your gastrointestinal tract hosts roughly 38 trillion microorganisms — bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses — that collectively make up the gut microbiome. This isn’t a passive passenger. The microbiome influences immune function, nutrient absorption, neurotransmitter production, and inflammatory response. Researchers have linked microbiome composition to conditions ranging from inflammatory bowel disease to depression.

What you eat shapes this community. And fermented foods may be one of the most direct ways to support microbial diversity.

item.title: Training for My First Marathon
item.description:
Why I Signed Up

I’d been running casually for two years — a few miles here, a 10K there — but never with a real goal. Signing up for a marathon was mostly an act of self-coercion. If I’d paid for a race, I’d actually train for it. The logic proved sound.

item.title: Vim Motions for Everyone
item.description:
The Modal Editing Model

Vim’s central idea is modal editing: the keyboard does different things depending on which mode you’re in. In Normal mode, keys are commands. In Insert mode, keys type text. In Visual mode, keys select text. This feels bizarre for the first few days and then becomes difficult to give up.

The benefit is that your hands rarely need to leave the home row. No reaching for the mouse. No arrow keys. No Ctrl+Shift gymnastics to select a word. Text editing becomes a composable language.

item.title: My Minimalist Productivity System
item.description:
The Trap of Productivity Optimization

There’s a special kind of procrastination that masquerades as productivity: endlessly optimizing your system instead of doing the work. I’ve rebuilt my task manager four times, tried every major note-taking app, and read more books about productivity than I’ve care to admit. The result was an elaborate system that required constant maintenance and gave me anxiety just looking at it.

The fix wasn’t a better tool. It was fewer tools.

item.title: How LLMs Actually Work
item.description:
Tokens, Not Words

The first thing to unlearn is that LLMs think in words. They don’t. They operate on tokens — chunks of text that might be a whole word, a syllable, a punctuation mark, or a common multi-word phrase. The word “unbelievable” might be three tokens; “cat” is one. This tokenization step is where raw text gets converted into integers that the model can actually process.

The Transformer Architecture

Modern LLMs are built on the Transformer architecture, introduced in the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need. The key innovation was the attention mechanism: a way for the model to weigh the relevance of every token in the context against every other token simultaneously.

item.title: Typography for the Web
item.description:
Why Typography Is the Foundation

Before color, before layout, before imagery — a web page is text. Most of what the web communicates travels through type. Getting typography right doesn’t mean picking a beautiful font; it means making reading effortless. When it works, readers don’t notice. When it fails, they leave.

The Core Variables

Line Length

Optimal line length for body text is 60–75 characters, including spaces. Too wide and the eye struggles to track back to the next line. Too narrow and the constant jumping creates visual noise. In CSS, max-width: 65ch on your content container is a reasonable starting point.

item.title: Dark Mode Design Principles
item.description:
Dark Mode Is Not an Inversion

The most common mistake is treating dark mode as a simple color flip: white becomes black, black becomes white. The result looks like a photo negative — jarring, flat, and hard to read for sustained periods. True dark mode design requires building a parallel visual system.

The key insight is that light and shadow work differently against dark backgrounds. On a white canvas, elements gain depth by darkening (shadows, borders, lower luminance). On a dark canvas, elements gain depth by lightening — slightly elevated surfaces appear closer to the viewer.

item.title: Sourdough From Scratch
item.description:
Starting the Starter

The first thing to understand about sourdough is that it’s not really about bread — it’s about building a living culture of wild yeast and bacteria. Before you bake anything, you need a starter: a mixture of flour and water that you feed daily until it becomes reliably active.

My recipe is simple. Mix 50g of whole wheat flour with 50g of room-temperature water in a clean jar. Cover loosely and leave it at room temperature. Each day, discard all but 50g of the mixture, then feed it with 50g flour and 50g water. After five to seven days you’ll see consistent bubbling and a pleasantly sour, almost fruity smell. Your starter is ready.

item.title: How GPS Works
item.description:
Thirty Satellites, One Location

The Global Positioning System consists of at least 24 operational satellites in medium Earth orbit, distributed so that at least four are above the horizon from anywhere on the planet at any given time. Each satellite continuously broadcasts a signal that includes two things: its precise location in orbit, and the exact time the signal was sent.

Your GPS receiver listens to these signals and measures how long each one took to arrive. Since radio waves travel at the speed of light (about 299,792 km/s), travel time × speed gives you distance. With distances from four or more satellites, the receiver can solve for three spatial coordinates plus its own clock error. This is called trilateration.

item.title: My Week in Kyoto
item.description:
Arriving in the Old Capital

Kyoto doesn’t announce itself the way Tokyo does. There’s no neon overload, no thunderous Shinkansen interchange to overwhelm you on arrival. The city reveals itself slowly — a moss-covered stone lantern here, a persimmon tree leaning over a clay wall there. I arrived on a Tuesday in April, one week before peak cherry blossom crowds, and the timing turned out to be perfect.

My base was a machiya guesthouse in the Nishiki neighborhood, a narrow wooden townhouse with paper screens, a tiny inner garden, and the faint smell of old cedar. It cost roughly the same as a mid-range hotel but felt like a completely different country.

item.title: Introduction to Docker
item.description:
The Problem Docker Solves

“It works on my machine” is one of the oldest complaints in software development. Differences in OS versions, library versions, environment variables, and file paths cause software that runs perfectly in development to fail mysteriously in production. Docker solves this by packaging your application and everything it needs — runtime, libraries, configuration — into a single portable unit called a container.

Containers vs. Virtual Machines

A common misconception is that containers are lightweight virtual machines. They’re not. A VM includes a full operating system, making it slow to start and heavy on resources. A container shares the host OS kernel and isolates only the application layer using Linux namespaces and cgroups. This makes containers start in milliseconds and use a fraction of the memory of a comparable VM.

item.title: Understanding CSS Grid
item.description:
The Layout Problem Grid Solves

Before Grid, web layouts were a series of creative hacks. We floated elements meant for text, abused tables for structure, and eventually leaned heavily on Flexbox — which, while excellent, is fundamentally one-dimensional. CSS Grid is the first native two-dimensional layout system built into the browser, and it changes what’s possible.

Core Concepts

Defining a Grid

Everything starts with the container:

.container {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: auto;
  gap: 1.5rem;
}

1fr is the key unit — it represents a fraction of available space, letting the browser handle the math. The gap property adds gutters between cells without you needing to fuss with margins.

item.title: The Rise of Edge Computing
item.description:
What Is Edge Computing?

For years, the story of modern infrastructure has been about centralization — moving data to massive cloud data centers where it can be processed at scale. Edge computing flips that narrative. Instead of shipping raw data to a distant server, edge computing moves the compute workload to the source of the data: a factory floor, a retail store, a cell tower, or even a device in your pocket.

item.title: A Brief History of the Internet
item.description:
It Wasn’t Invented to Survive a Nuclear War

That’s the myth, anyway. ARPANET — the US Defense Department research network that became the internet’s ancestor — was funded by the military, but its actual designers were university researchers trying to solve a much more mundane problem: how to share expensive computing resources across institutions without driving to each other’s campuses.

The first ARPANET message was sent on October 29, 1969, between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute. The intended message was “login.” The system crashed after “lo.” An accidental first word for a network that would eventually carry everything.

item.title: Getting Started with Rust: A Beginner's Guide
item.description:
Rust has taken the programming world by storm, consistently topping developer satisfaction surveys. But what makes it worth learning?

Why Rust?

Rust solves a problem that has plagued systems programmers for decades: how do you write fast, low-level code without sacrificing memory safety? Languages like C and C++ give you raw performance but leave you responsible for every allocation and deallocation. One mistake and you’re debugging a segfault at 2am.
